q: A founder planning a booking app for mobile dog groomers lists these assumptions. Which should she test first?
options: She can build a booking calendar that works well on any kind of phone
Groomers will pay a monthly fee rather than use free messaging apps
Dog owners care a lot about their dogs being clean and well groomed
Groomers will want to use the app in more than one language
why: If groomers won't pay, nothing else matters, and she has no evidence either way. A booking calendar is known to be buildable, owners' care is well established, and language support only matters if the rest works.

q: Which interview question is most likely to give you reliable information?
options: Would you use an app that reminds you when to reorder stock?
How much would you pay for a tool that solved this for you?
Don't you find it frustrating to keep track of stock on paper?
When did you last run out of stock, and what did you do?
why: A question about a specific recent event gets you facts about real behavior. The others ask for a prediction, a guessed price or agreement, which people often give just to be polite.

q: After you describe your idea, which response is the strongest evidence of real demand?
options: They pay a small deposit to be among the first users
They say it's brilliant and that you should definitely build it
They ask you to let them know as soon as it launches
They say they'd probably use it most weeks
why: A deposit costs the person something, so it's a commitment rather than a compliment. Praise, interest and predictions cost nothing and are easy to give out of kindness.

q: You want to know whether busy parents will pay for weekly meal plans before you build any software. What's a good first test?
options: Build the full app with recipe recommendations, then see who signs up
Post an online survey asking parents whether they like the idea
Make plans yourself for a few families who've paid, and email them
Research every competitor for a month before talking to anyone
why: A paid, hand-delivered version tests the riskiest question, whether people will pay and keep using it, in days rather than months. A survey collects opinions, and building first is the most expensive way to find out.

q: Why should you set a success threshold before you run a test?
options: So you have a precise, impressive number to show investors later
So you can't quietly change what counts as success after seeing the results
So you only run the tests you're already confident you'll pass
Because a test finishes faster when there's a number attached
why: After seeing results, it's tempting to read a weak response as encouraging. A threshold written down in advance keeps you honest about what you learned.
